blocks.x: Twenty-five years ago, the remote Newfoundland town of Gander found itself becoming an unlikely haven at the edge of the North Atlantic. In the wake of 9/11, more than 4,000 airborne flights were forced to divert when the Federal Aviation Administration closed American airspace—and 38 of those aircraft landed in Gander, bringing nearly 7,000 passengers and crew to a town of just 10,000 people.

Brian Mosher, a Gander resident and TV reporter, filmed practically non-stop in the days following September 11, in an attempt to share what was happening on the ground with the world. “There were 7,000 different reasons why people had to get home,” says Mosher. “We were their shoulders to cry on.”

The “come from aways,” the Newfoundland term for out-of-towners, were welcomed into the community with warmth, love, food, and anything else their hosts could provide. Buffet tables were set up to feed the new arrivals, and accommodation arranged in homes, schools, and churches. “We thought we’d give them a bite to eat before we put them back on their planes, not realizing they were going to have to stay here five days,” he says. The events of these confusing, confounding days went on to inspire a hit Broadway musical, Come From Away, with Ganderites immortalized in song.

Today, Gander International Airport feels smaller and sleepier than its reputation might suggest. Most travelers who find themselves here are on brief stopovers en route to or from other destinations in Newfoundland and Labrador. Others have made a special visit, drawn by the extraordinary architecture and design of the former International Departures Terminal, a Modernist time capsule dating back to 1959.

Gander Airport’s legacy actually far predates the events of 9/11–in fact, going all the way back to a time when global aviation was, literally, just taking off. It was the late 1930s, just three decades after Orville and Wilbur Wright’s first flight took off from Kitty Hawk beach in North Carolina. With long-haul air travel underway, and Newfoundland’s location on the Great Circle Route—930 miles closer to Europe than anywhere else in North America—positioned Gander as the perfect staging point for refueling, maintenance, and emergencies at a time when flying was far more unpredictable and potentially unreliable than we know it to be today

The first plane to land in Gander touched down on a snow-packed runway in 1938. By 1940, it was already the world’s largest airport, and in World War II served as the main maintenance point for Allied aircraft flying to Europe. Eventually, Gander would go on to welcome commercial flights from Europe and the Soviet Union for refueling stops, but it couldn’t throw off its military past. Until 1959, arriving travelers still found themselves disembarking into a hangar designed for WWII.

Newfoundland Department of Tourism

The opening of the Gander Airport International Departures Terminal by Queen Elizabeth II in June that year changed everything. The new terminal was a showcase for an ambitious, modernizing, young nation featuring Canadian Modernist art and design, as well as stylish furniture by some of the design world’s greatest names like Charles and Ray Eames and Arne Jacobsen. Gander was now ready to welcome world leaders, celebrities, royalty, and rock stars to this little outpost in remote eastern Newfoundland, and was determined to put on a show. Major stars of the day passed through—Marilyn Monroe, Albert Einstein, and Elizabeth Taylor—and could be seen drinking martinis at the Big Dipper, Newfoundland’s only 24-hour bar.

As the Jet Age advanced and aircraft became more powerful with increased ranges, trans-Atlantic flights no longer needed to make refueling stops. Arrivals into what was once the “crossroads of the world” began to slow, and Gander’s fortunes declined. The glamorous international terminal and lounge, no longer a necessity, was at risk of being lost to a newer, smaller, more economical option. Eventually, an outpouring of support led to its rescue, and in 2022 it reopened as a museum space with a small movie theater, gastropub, and souvenir shop.

Newfoundland Department of Tourism

Today, it is preserved largely as it was in its heyday. The Mondrian-esque terrazzo floor in shades of salmon, slate, and jade still carries the sheen of 1950s glamour. Clocks on the wall still tell the time in London, Montreal, New York, and Moscow. Stylized bird sculptures by Arthur Price welcoming arriving passengers to Canada still gather in a flock. But the most dramatic feature is the 72-foot Flight and Its Allegories mural by Canadian artist Kenneth Lochhead, featuring a dynamic scene of activity and abundance. A matronly figure stands with arms outstretched. A bearded man feeds airplane-shaped bluebirds. A boy peers through binoculars. Stylized birds burst into the air, some Concorde-like in form, predating the iconic supersonic aircraft by over a decade.
“In a way, it was like Penn Station in New York, but for the world"

Gander-born Todd Saunders, the celebrated architect behind Newfoundland modern icon Fogo Island Inn, credits the International Departure Terminal as being his first exposure to contemporary architecture. “The Canadian government invested in architecture because this was the first face of Canada, and that first impression was really important,” he says.

But the airport’s pull went beyond architecture alone. Saunders still recalls the smell of Cuban cigars that lingered after flights stopped in en route between Havana and Moscow. “In a way, it was like Penn Station in New York, but for the world,” he says. The international terminal used to be open to the public at the time, and in doing so, held a cosmopolitan allure for the people of Gander. “My dad worked there as an airplane mechanic and he would call me and say, ‘The [Rolling] Stones are here’, and I’d get on my BMX and head down. You’d be looking at Mick Jagger because they’d had to stop for gas," he recalls.
